## What it is

The cradle `screen_wedge` sits in, so the screen stands at `tilt` (45° by default) against
a vertical surface the base is plaqued against — `footing` at 0 drops the back face
straight down from the ridge instead of sloping back onto a desk, see below. A hollow
wedge box printed **fond on the bed**, empty seen from above, with the electronics
under the screen. The wedge is not fastened to it: it slides down between two rails
onto two pins and is held by its own weight. **The wedge is also the lid**, and the
only way in. Two side panels close over its full 19.6 mm thickness and press-fit onto
`wedge_width`, hiding the USB-C openings `screen_wedge` cuts into its own border.

About **2 h 16 m and 93 g** on the A1 Mini, and it holds roughly 5300× the screen's
weight — this part is nowhere near its strength limit, see below.

## Design notes

- **Why this exists at all.** `screen_wedge` cannot be printed in one piece with its
  own support. Laid on a 60° seat the monolith gives **17 findings, 13 of them
  blocking**: 2 849.9 mm² of 60° overhang, a 107 mm bridge over 1 652.2 mm² which is
  the pocket ceiling the module fits against, a 74 mm bridge over 111.0 mm², and 8
  regions whose first layer starts in mid-air. The two constraints are exclusive: the
  seat wants 60°, the pocket and its walls want ≤ 45°. There is no compromise angle.
  Both reference designs found online split the same way — Waveshare's own is a case
  plus a separate stand, octopint is four screwed panels.
- **`backing` is the parameter, and the ridge height is computed from it.**
  `north_height = seat_height + backing·sin(tilt)`. Backing is how much of the wedge's
  77.8 mm actually lies on the slope, and it is the number with meaning: at **77.8 the
  whole wedge is backed**, so a press anywhere on the glass is pure compression into
  the slope. 63.5 backs only the touchscreen, and below that the top of the active area
  overhangs the ridge, where a **2.46 N** press rocks the screen off its seat — inside
  the range of a firm touch. `reject` guards both ends of that range.
- **Why the ridge is not a parameter.** Any two of {ridge height, tilt, backing} fix the
  third, and the ridge is the one nobody chooses on purpose. As a free number it drifted
  silently: raising `seat_height` 10 mm cut backing to 66.3 mm unless you also raised the
  ridge, and `screen_assembly`'s `tilt` slider — which passes tilt down but never passed
  a ridge height — swung backing from **95.3 mm at 45° to 69.8 mm at 75°** with nothing
  in the viewer saying so. Computed from `backing`, both sliders leave the screen's
  support alone.
- **The lip is the wedge's thickness, 19.60 mm, measured perpendicular to the seat.**
  That is what makes it flush with the glass: it hides no part of the module, whose
  own bottom bezel is 9.09 mm anyway.
- **The lip is never a full-width plate.** As a plate its underside is a 30° downward
  face over **2 470 mm²**. It lives on the side walls and on two ergots, each a solid
  triangle standing on the floor whose own underside falls at 49.7°.
- **The rebate is what stops the screen moving sideways during the slide.** Each side
  wall is a 4 mm shelf whose top lies on the seat, for the wedge's border to rest on,
  plus a 2 mm rail standing 3 mm proud of it. `channel_fit` 0.4 leaves 0.2 mm a side —
  loose on purpose, so the wedge still slides freely down onto the pins.
- **The side panels are a separate job: hiding the USB-C openings, not the slide fit.**
  `rail_height` (3 mm) only ever had to stop sideways play; `screen_wedge`'s own
  border is 19.6 mm thick, so above the rail its USB-C/UART channel openings were
  exposed straight out the side. `side_panel_depth` (19.6, the wedge's full thickness)
  closes over them, and `side_panel_fit` (−0.1mm total) is measured off `wedge_width`
  itself rather than the loose `channel_fit`, so the wedge presses into the last bit of
  its travel instead of rattling.
- **The panel follows the wedge's own back corner exactly, flush — it is not chamfered.**
  That corner reads as a sharp near-90° peak standing proud of the ridge, but cutting a
  chamfer into it there recedes the panel behind the wedge, which fills right up to
  the same corner: tried, and it opened a visible triangular gap along the join instead
  of softening anything. `screen_wedge` drops the polish chamfer on its own outer rim
  perimeter (`on_outer_rim`) for the same reason, so the two land flush with no reveal
  either side of the join. `seating()` also excludes this face's edges from polish here,
  same as the seat and lip planes.
- **Neither the panel's inner (mating) face nor the shelf's inner face is chamfered —
  both are faces the wedge presses or rests flush against, and a bevel anywhere on
  their perimeter breaks that line.** `on_flat_face(edge, x)` excludes any edge lying
  flat on a face perpendicular to X at `±x`, used for the panel's inner face at
  `press_half` and the shelf's inner face at `channel_half - shelf_width`, rather than
  naming individual edges on either. An earlier version (`on_panel_return`) only
  targeted the ridge-return edge by checking `on_plane(edge, ridge, up)` restricted to
  that X — it missed the longer edge running from the front wall's crest up to the
  ridge, which is not one of the profile's named points but an edge the boolean union
  creates there; that one kept its chamfer and showed as a diagonal bevel band down
  the whole inner face. The same gap existed on the shelf's own inner edge, where the
  wedge's border actually lands. Checking the X-plane directly instead of guessing at
  each edge's shape catches the whole perimeter of either face in one test, including
  edges no per-edge check anticipated. The notch relief is handled separately,
  unaffected: it's still built before the panel is added, so the cut never nicks the
  panel's own face.
- **The foot pins run along the slope, not normal to it.** Along the slope they lean
  30° off vertical, so their own underside sits at 60° and prints support-free. Normal
  to the seat they would lean 60° and overhang at 30°.
- **`footing` 0 is the default: the base is plaqued against a vertical surface**, so the
  back face drops straight down from the ridge (90° at the bottom-right corner in
  side view) instead of sloping back to a desk. Raise `footing` past 0 to go back to
  the free-standing desk version below, where the sloped back face plus its
  `footing_edge` tip is what resists tipping.
- **There is no notch relief cut.** An earlier version had one — 0.5 mm square along the
  notch line, meant as the doctrine's inside-corner relief at a load-bearing junction —
  but its box shared an exact X boundary with the rail's inner face at `channel_half`,
  and that tangency tessellated into a visible glitch at the seam once the panel's own
  inner chamfer stopped covering it (see the polish notes above and the changelog). The
  wedge's own bottom-rear edge sits on the bed in its print pose, so polish never
  touches it there and it comes out sharp regardless; nothing was actually perching on
  the corner. Removing the cut settled the glitch and dropped the part's two
  previously-accepted slivers to zero.
- **Nothing the wedge touches is chamfered.** `seating()` pulls every edge lying on the
  seat plane or the lip plane out of the polish pass, because a 1 mm chamfer there is
  1 mm of daylight under the screen. Every other edge keeps its 1 mm chamfer.
- **Breaking is nowhere close either way.** `nurb stress` gives ~5300× margin and
  0.0002 mm of sag at the default `footing` 0.
- **Free-standing (`footing` > 0): tipping was the failure mode, not breaking.** With
  the screen on board (236 g all in, module at 115 g) the assembly tipped at about
  **2.6 N** at the top of the active area at `footing` 30, and a firm touch is 1 to 3 N.
  `footing` 40 buys 3.4 N. 10 mm more footing is +0.86 N. Dropping `tilt` to 45° is
  +5 mm of depth, −8 mm of height and **+46 %** of tipping resistance versus 60°,
  because it lowers the centre of gravity as well as lengthening the base. None of
  this applies against a wall: the vertical back face at `footing` 0 bears on the wall
  directly, so there is no tipping mode to buy margin against.
- `seat_height` 30 mm is the room under the screen for the electronics. Because the
  ridge rises with it, depth is unchanged —
  `depth = 19.6·sin(tilt) + backing·cos(tilt) + footing` does not mention it.
- **At `footing` > 0 the back face's angle belongs to the ridge height and `footing`,
  not to `tilt`.** At ridge 97.38 over a 30 mm footing it falls at **72.2°**, steeper
  than the 70.2° it had at ridge 87.4, and still self-supporting either way.

## Don't

- **Don't merge this back into `screen_wedge`.** The monolith is 13 blocking findings,
  and the supports land inside the pocket on the module's 0.5 mm fit surface and across
  the four M2.5 counterbores, which end up bored at 30° to the bed.
- **Don't make the lip a full-width plate** "so the screen bears evenly". It is a 30°
  downward face over 2 470 mm². The ergots exist for exactly this reason.
- **Don't put pins normal to the seat**, at the top corners or anywhere. Tried: 2 fails
  at 22 mm² each of 30° overhang, and there is nothing under them to corbel onto. The
  rebate does that job with no holes in the wedge at all.
- **Don't add a transverse wall under the ridge.** It was in for one revision. Measured
  against no wall at all: 0.019 mm of sag versus 0.017, margin 305× versus 307× — **2 %**
  — and it blocks component placement and cable runs. The shear panel that keeps an
  open-top shell square is the wedge itself, once seated.
- **Don't make the side profile a V or a tent.** The wedge would slide off. The lip and
  the low front wall are what catch it.
- **Don't reach for magnets here.** They were the original plan and every job they had
  is now done by geometry: the lip stops the slide, the rails stop the sideways play,
  the pins locate, and full backing stops the rocking. Magnets
  only ever helped tipping, and only against a magnetic support.
- **Don't chamfer the seat slope or the lip face**, and don't "fix" the sharp edges they
  leave. They are the faces the screen lies on.
- **Don't bring `north_height` back as a parameter.** It was one until 2026-08-21 and it
  drifted every time `seat_height` or `tilt` moved, silently changing what holds the
  screen up. `backing` says the same thing in the units that matter and the ridge falls
  out of it.
- **Don't tighten the pin fit.** 5.5 mm sockets on 5 mm pins is a free fit on purpose:
  two pins 60 mm apart on two separately printed parts will not meet a snug fit.
- **Don't chamfer the side panels' top-back corner** where they meet the wedge, even
  though it looks like a sharp spike. Tried, at 8 mm: it opened a visible triangular
  gap along the join because the wedge fills right up to that same corner and the
  panel no longer reached it. Fix any pointedness there on `screen_wedge`'s own edge
  instead, matching what `on_outer_rim` already does — never on the panel's face.
- **Don't bring the notch relief cut back**, at `channel_half`, at `press_half`, or
  widened by a small overlap epsilon — all three were tried. Sized to `channel_half`
  it sat exactly tangent with the rail's inner face and tessellated into a visible
  glitch at the seam; resized to `press_half` the same tangency just moved into the
  shelf's own body instead; widened by 0.1 mm past `channel_half` it still left the
  same sub-mm² tangent slivers, only shifted. Nothing was perching on the corner
  without it — the wedge's bottom-rear edge sits on the bed in its own print pose, so
  polish never touched that edge either way. Removing the cut entirely is what
  actually cleared it.

## Changelog

- 2026-09-04: notch relief cut (`fit`) removed entirely, and the parameter with it.
  It sat exactly tangent with the rail's inner face at `channel_half`, and once the
  panel's own inner chamfer stopped masking that seam (previous entry), the tangency
  showed as a visible glitch at the notch. Widening the cut by a small overlap epsilon
  only moved the same sub-mm² tangent slivers rather than removing them; dropping the
  cut did. 52 → 42 faces, checks clean, zero slivers — the 2 previously accepted are
  gone. `screen_assembly`'s stale `tilt` default (60°, from before `screen_base`'s own
  default moved to 45°) fixed to match in the same pass.
- 2026-09-04: `on_flat_face(edge, x)` now also excludes the shelf's inner face
  (`channel_half - shelf_width`) from polish, matching the panel's. Same bug as the
  panel below: nothing had named the shelf's own inner edge, so it kept a chamfer
  where the wedge's border actually lands.
- 2026-09-04: `on_panel_return` replaced by `on_panel_inner` (later generalised to
  `on_flat_face`), which excludes the panel's whole inner face (`X = ±press_half`)
  from polish instead of naming the ridge-return edge alone. The narrower check missed
  a diagonal edge from the front wall's crest up to the ridge — not one of the
  profile's named points, so it never matched `on_plane(edge, ridge, up)` — and it
  kept its chamfer, showing as a visible bevel band running the height of each inner
  panel face. 64 → 60 faces.
- 2026-09-04: two more internal edges dropped from the polish pass — the panel's
  return to the ridge (`on_panel_return`) and, by reordering the notch relief cut
  before the panels are added instead of after, the panel's mating face no longer
  gets nicked by that cut either. Both were chamfers with no purpose, on faces a
  square box slides against; the first one also opened a visible gap along the
  wedge join. Traded for 2 accepted sub-mm² slivers where the relief cut and the
  rail's inner face sit exactly tangent — see `[accepted]` above.
- 2026-09-04: two side panels added, closing over `screen_wedge`'s full 19.6 mm
  thickness (`side_panel_depth`) and press-fitting onto `wedge_width`
  (`side_panel_fit` −0.1mm total), to hide the USB-C/UART openings that show above
  the low rail. Flush against the wedge's own outer rim, which dropped its polish
  chamfer there to match (see `screen_wedge`'s changelog). `footing` default 30 → 0:
  the back face now drops straight from the ridge for mounting against a vertical
  surface instead of sloping back onto a desk; raise `footing` for the free-standing
  desk version. 130.50 × 85.87 × 98.38 → 130.50 × 68.87 × 98.87 mm, 2 h 28 m / 101 g
  → 2 h 20 m / 93 g, and the one previously-accepted sliver is gone (see above for
  the two new ones).
- 2026-08-21: `north_height` replaced by `backing` (77.8, the whole wedge), with the
  ridge computed as `seat_height + backing·sin(tilt)`. Geometry is the same to 0.02 mm,
  which is the old hand-rounded 97.4 against the exact 97.38.
- 2026-08-21: `seat_height` 20 → 30 for more room under the screen, and `north_height`
  87.4 → 97.4 with it, because the backing is set by the difference of the two and the
  wedge has to stay fully backed. Depth unchanged at 85.89, height 88.40 → 98.40,
  +14.7 % volume, 2 h 28 m / 101 g. Back face steepens 70.2° → 72.2°; `footing` left at
  30, so tipping is now the looser of the two margins.
- 2026-08-17: first cut. Hollow cradle, fond on the bed, seat backing all 77.8 mm of
  the wedge, lip on two ergots, side rebate with rails, two foot pins, 30 mm footing
  under a back face falling at 70.2°. 130.50 × 85.89 × 88.40 mm, checks clean bar one
  accepted sliver, 2 h 03 m / 84 g. Replaces the earlier rectangular electronics bay
  with four magnet towers, which predated the decision to carry the screen on a slope.
